questions.q: What is pushing toward the cloud: a data-centre exit, recovery, peak demand, or sovereignty?
questions.why: The driver decides which proof matters.
questions.need: The reason to use cloud capacity is written down and agreed
questions.how: Name the driver with the sponsor and the date that matters
questions.listen: Each driver points to a different design: an exit needs migration, recovery needs a standby, peaks need bursting.
questions.probe: If the cloud cost the same as today, would you still move, and why?

questions.q: Which data must stay in a country or under a given jurisdiction, and who checks it?
questions.why: Sovereignty requirements shape every design choice.
questions.need: The data with residency rules is known, with the rule and who checks it
questions.how: List the data with residency rules and the evidence each needs
questions.listen: Sovereignty narrows regions and providers: name the rule and who audits it.
questions.probe: Who approved the current cloud contracts from a data-protection point of view?

questions.q: Which cloud accounts and clusters exist today, and who manages them?
questions.why: Cloud capacity run apart is where policies drift.
questions.need: Every cloud cluster is known and managed with the data centre
questions.how: List cloud accounts and attach their clusters to the same management
questions.listen: Accounts opened by teams without IT are both a cost leak and a security gap.
questions.probe: How many cloud accounts show up on expense reports rather than central contracts?

questions.q: Can workloads keep their addresses when they move, or must they be changed?
questions.why: Re-addressing is what turns a move into a project.
questions.need: The network design lets workloads move without changing addresses
questions.how: Agree the network extension design with the network team
questions.listen: Keeping addresses avoids touching applications, firewall rules and licences; changing them multiplies the work.
questions.probe: Which applications have addresses written into their configuration or licences?

questions.q: Has a failover to the cloud been run, and how long did it take?
questions.why: Cloud recovery is only real once tested.
questions.need: A failover to the cloud has been run and met its objectives
questions.how: Run a test failover of one application to the cloud
questions.listen: A failover never run takes longer than its runbook says.
questions.probe: Which step was slowest, and was it technical or a decision?

questions.q: Do the same security rules apply in the cloud as in the data centre?
questions.why: Different rules in two places means gaps in both.
questions.need: Security policies follow workloads wherever they run
questions.how: Compare policies in both places and close the differences
questions.listen: Two rule sets drift apart; one policy that follows the workload closes the gap.
questions.probe: Who maintains the cloud firewall rules, and are they reviewed with the data-centre ones?

questions.q: Is cloud capacity paid for when nothing runs on it?
questions.why: Idle capacity is where cloud budgets go.
questions.need: Idle cloud capacity is hibernated or released by policy
questions.how: Set a policy for idle clusters and measure the saving
questions.listen: Standby capacity paid around the clock is the first saving to model.
questions.probe: What does idle or standby cloud capacity cost each month?

questions.q: Who decides what runs where, and reviews the cloud bill?
questions.why: Without an owner, hybrid becomes two estates.
questions.need: A named owner decides placement and reviews cloud cost monthly
questions.how: Name the owner and set a monthly review
questions.listen: Without an owner for placement, workloads land wherever was easiest at the time.
questions.probe: When was a workload last brought back from the cloud, and why?

questions.q: Could a small cluster in the cloud wait for a disaster, and grow only when one happens?
questions.why: Paying for a full second site that sits idle is what makes recovery expensive.
questions.need: A small standing cluster in the cloud grows at failover, and the time it takes to grow has been tested
questions.how: Size the smallest standing cluster and time adding servers during a test failover
questions.listen: A small standby that grows only when needed makes cloud recovery affordable.
questions.probe: How quickly must recovery capacity be there after a disaster is declared?

questions.q: Which cloud providers do you already have commitments with, and how much of them is unused?
questions.why: Unused commitments are budget already spent: workloads that consume them cost less than they seem.
questions.need: The cloud commitments in place are known, with what is left and until when
questions.how: List the commitments per provider, with what each has left
questions.listen: Unused prepaid commitments can fund the move: often the fastest business case.
questions.probe: When do those commitments expire, and what happens to what is unused?

questions.q: Which projects are on hold because servers are late or not yet priced?
questions.why: A project on hold for servers is the clearest case for capacity that can be rented within days.
questions.need: Projects on hold for hardware are listed, with what each month of delay costs
questions.how: List the projects on hold and the date their servers are expected
questions.listen: Projects waiting for hardware show what speed is worth.
questions.probe: What does a month of delay cost the project that has waited longest?

questions.q: Which software is licensed per core, and where would it cost least to run?
questions.why: Operating system and database licences can change the cost of a cloud more than the servers do.
questions.need: Per-core licences are counted for every place a workload could run
questions.how: Count the licensed cores for operating systems and databases, workload by workload
questions.listen: Licences priced per core can cost more in the cloud than the infrastructure: run them where they cost least.
questions.probe: Which licence agreements allow use on dedicated cloud hosts?

questions.q: Does the cloud provider fund assessments or migrations for this move, and has anyone asked?
questions.why: Provider programmes can pay for part of a move, and are easier to get early than late.
questions.need: Funding available from the provider is known and requested at the start
questions.how: Ask the provider's account team which programmes apply, before the plan is fixed
questions.listen: Providers often fund assessments and migration effort; it is worth asking early.
questions.probe: Who is your account manager at the provider, and do they know about this project?

questions.q: Which applications regularly send data out of the cloud, and what does that traffic cost?
questions.why: Charges for data leaving the cloud, and latency, decide what should stay together.
questions.need: Traffic leaving the cloud and its cost are known per application
questions.how: Read the data-transfer lines of the last cloud bill by application
questions.listen: Chatty applications split across places pay twice: in transfer charges and in latency.
questions.probe: Which application's cloud bill surprised you most this year?

questions.q: How are the data centres and the cloud connected today: private links, VPN, bandwidth, and who pays?
questions.why: The connection limits what can move, how fast, and at what cost.
questions.need: Links between sites and clouds are documented with their bandwidth
questions.how: List links, bandwidth and contracts between sites and clouds
questions.listen: A single VPN is enough for a pilot, not for recovering production: plan the link with the use case.
questions.probe: What is the lead time to order a faster private link?

questions.q: Should the same people, tools and processes run workloads in the data centre and in the cloud?
questions.why: One way of operating both is where hybrid saves the most effort.
questions.need: One way of operating is agreed for both places
questions.how: Map which tools and teams run each environment today
questions.listen: Two teams with two toolsets is the cost hybrid should remove; keeping both shrinks the savings.
questions.probe: Which task is done twice today, once in each environment?
